recommendation: Pick Godot 4 .NET. For a new developer building a menu-heavy 2D strategy game for desktop, Godot is free, light and quick to iterate in, its Control/container UI suits the roster, stock, build and card screens, and TileMapLayer handles both the hex State Map and the isometric battle grid. Its weak spots for this project (fewer C# tutorials, C# web export not yet available) do not matter for a desktop-only game. The decision stays reversible because everything that is hard (the 410-module sim's rules, AI, content, saves, determinism) lives in an engine-free C# library with its own tests, written to C# 9/netstandard2.1 so Unity can compile it too: the Godot project is only a thin SimHost bridge plus screens. If you ever prefer Unity, you rewrite the bridge and the screens (cards in L4) and keep the sim, content and save files untouched.

workflow: Pick the next card on the board, move it to Doing, and create a branch: git switch -c feat/core.clock
Data first: add or extend the JSON content and its C# record (e.g. a building's cost in buildings.json + BuildingDef), and run the content validation test
Write a failing xUnit test that states the rule in plain terms ('a Lodge with 12 wood queued finishes after 8 work-hours')
Implement the sim rule (a system or command handler) until the test passes; keep it engine-free
Run the fast tests (dotnet test --filter Category!=Slow) and the determinism/save tests for the area you touched
Try it headless: tools/Headless --seed 42 --days 7 and read the daily summary/log for nonsense
Wire a placeholder UI: a command button (with Check() reason tooltip) and a label/list driven by an event or query via SimHost
Playtest for 10 minutes in the engine with dev tools (give, step, reveal); write any surprise as a new test
Commit in small steps with clear messages; push the branch
Open a PR into dev with the card's checklist; CI must be green; review your own diff
Merge, move the card to Done, update the card if the real numbers differ from the plan

layers.name: Data (database)
layers.what: Static content in content/*.json (items, terrain, buildings, dead, loot tables, cards) loaded into immutable C# records by ContentDb, plus the runtime World model that a save file stores. Together: the game's database, with no server.
layers.rules: No logic beyond validation. IDs are forever. Every reference checked by tests. Art only as string art keys. Per-game values (condition, ammo left) live in state, never in definitions.

layers.name: Backend (sim)
layers.what: BrokenState.Sim: systems run hourly/daily in a fixed order, command handlers validate and apply player/AI intents, AI and battle rules, seeded RNG streams, saves.
layers.rules: No engine references (enforced by a test). Deterministic: only sim Rng, ordered iteration, no wall-clock time. Changes only through commands and ticks; reports only through events and queries. Unit-tested before any UI.

layers.name: Bridge
layers.what: SimHost (Godot autoload / Unity MonoBehaviour): owns the Game, converts real time to game hours at the chosen speed, drains events into signals/C# events, turns input into commands, builds view models.
layers.rules: Thin: no game rules. One instance. Does not cache sim objects across frames; re-queries by ID. Engine pause is separate from sim pause.

layers.name: UI / presentation
layers.what: Screens and widgets (State Map, hub, team, cards, inventory, battle) that read view models and send commands; placeholder visuals via the ArtCatalog.
layers.rules: Never mutates World. Buttons call Check() for disabled-reason tooltips and Send() to act. Subscribes/unsubscribes to events with the node/component lifetime. Cosmetic randomness only.

layers.name: Art & audio (human-made, late)
layers.what: Final sprites, tiles, icons, UI skin, fonts, music and SFX made by humans in M8, slotted into the ArtCatalog/audio map under the same keys as the placeholders.
layers.rules: Zero code change to swap: same art keys, same sizes/pivots as agreed in the style guide. Stored via Git LFS. Licences recorded per asset. Placeholders (Kenney CC0) until then.

glossary.def: The basic building block in Godot: everything (a sprite, a button, a timer) is a node in a tree. Scripts attach to nodes.
A saved tree of nodes (.tscn) you can instance many times, like a prefab; a whole screen or a single button can be a scene.
A node or script Godot creates at startup and keeps alive across scene changes: Godot's singleton. SimHost is one.
Godot's built-in observer: a node emits a named signal and connected methods run. Like a C# event, also connectable in the editor.
A data object saved as .tres/.res with inspector-editable fields (textures, themes, custom data). Here: the ArtCatalog, not game rules.
Unity's basic object in a scene; on its own it does nothing until components are added.
The base class for Unity scripts attached to GameObjects, with lifecycle methods (Awake, Start, Update, OnEnable, OnDestroy).
A saved, reusable GameObject template (with its children and components) you instantiate at runtime.
An asset that holds data editable in the inspector, not attached to a scene. Here: art lookups and engine config, not game state.
Assembly Definition file: makes a folder compile into its own DLL; 'No Engine References' forbids UnityEngine, keeping the sim pure.
Seconds since the last frame. Used to turn frame time into game time in the bridge; never used inside sim rules.
One step of the simulation. In Broken State the campaign ticks one game-hour at a time, with a daily pass at midnight.
Same seed + same commands = exactly the same game. Makes bugs reproducible and tests meaningful.
The number that starts a pseudo-random sequence; a run's seed rebuilds its map and dice.
A separate seeded generator per system (map, weather, loot, battle) so one system's dice don't shift another's.
A pathfinding algorithm that finds the cheapest route by exploring tiles ordered by cost so far + an estimate to the goal.
Two numbers (q, r) on a hex grid where neighbour and distance math is simple; stored maps often use offset (column, row) and convert.
Hexes stored in rows like a 2D array, every odd row shifted half a hex; how the prototype stores tiles (id = y × width + x).
Something that is always in exactly one named state (e.g. a battle: PlayerTurn, EnemyTurn, Resolving, Ended) with clear rules for moving between states.
Entity-Component-System: data stored in packed component arrays processed by systems; great for tens of thousands of moving things. Not needed here: hundreds of survivors work fine as plain classes.
A place where the sim posts facts ('SurvivorDied') for others to react to later, so producers don't need to know who listens.
Representing an action as an object (QueueBuild) that can be validated, applied, logged, replayed or sent by AI.
Turning objects into text/bytes (JSON) and back; how saves and content files work.
A step that upgrades an old save (or content) from version n to n+1 when the data shape changes, so old saves still load.
Large File Storage: Git keeps small pointers in the repo and stores big binaries (art, audio) separately.
Continuous Integration: a server that builds and tests every push automatically.
A small automated check of one piece of logic in isolation (one rule, one function).
A test that compares output to a saved, approved result (e.g. a world digest after 7 days); changes must be re-approved on purpose.
A short fingerprint (rounded numbers or a hash) of a world's state, used to compare two runs quickly.
A thin but complete version of the game through every layer (map, base, travel, battle, save), playable end to end, before widening any one part.
Temporary visuals (coloured hexes, Kenney CC0 sprites) used until human-made art is ready.
A string like 'item.pistol_9mm' that content refers to; the engine's ArtCatalog maps it to the current sprite, so art swaps need no code.
Drawing a square grid rotated 45° and squashed (typically 2:1) to look 3D from above; used for the battle view.
Hiding tiles the player hasn't seen (or can't currently see); the sim tracks knowledge, the UI draws the fog.
AI that scores each possible action (attack, flee, eat) with formulas and picks the best; good for survival needs and the dead's choices.
AI as a tree of tasks and conditions evaluated top-down (sequence, selector); readable for scripted enemy behaviour.
Putting what varies (items, numbers, cards) in data files so designers change the game without changing code.
A small read-only record built for a screen (e.g. SurvivorRow: name, health %, job) so UI never touches the live state.
The thin engine-side layer that owns the sim, ticks it, forwards input as commands and events as signals.
Running the game logic without graphics or a window, e.g. in tests, CI or balance runs.
Drawing between two known sim states (a party at 14:00 and 15:00) so movement looks smooth while rules stay in whole hours.

learningPath.step: 1. C# basics: types, classes, records, collections, LINQ, nullable references
2. .NET projects and tests: solutions, class libraries, xUnit, dotnet test
3. Git and GitHub: commits, branches, PRs, LFS
4. Game architecture patterns: game loop, command, observer, event queue, type object
5. Engine basics: nodes/scenes, signals, autoloads, C# in Godot (or Unity Essentials)
6. Build the data + sim core headless (cards 7–18): content, state, RNG, saves, clock, events, commands, hexes, mapgen

portingFromPrototype: Treat the prototype as the spec, not the code to translate: read a module's header comment (the first 20–40 lines explain the rules and numbers) and the matching docs/features/<area>.md section, then design the C# version cleanly.

Its tests in prototype/tools/*test*.js are acceptance criteria: each header lists what it checks (e.g. weathertest: 28-day seasons, determinism, ETA exactness; savetest: save at half time, load, identical ending). Rewrite the important checks as xUnit tests, smaller and faster.

Copy the numbers, not the formulas' tangles: TERRAIN costs (walk 1 h/tile, vehicle 0.5, road 0.25), 1× = 20 s per game hour, speeds 0.5/1/2/3/5, TRAY_HOURS = 8, 4 × 28-day seasons with day 1 = spring day 15, map sizes 150 × 75 to 500 × 300. Put them in content JSON so they can be retuned.
Keep the same tick order for the systems you port (world.js hourOfWorld lists every hourly and daily step with a reason); the order encodes many hard-won fixes.

Keep determinism habits: separate RNG streams (weather never draws from the main dice), hash dice for per-tile features, IDs local to the world. Porting mulberry32 bit-for-bit lets you compare sequences with the prototype if useful.

Do NOT port: closures in event cards (they make open cards unsaveable: use effect records), the graph-shaped save with shared references (use IDs and a tree), process-wide id counters, the HTML-string UI and the giant main.js dispatcher (use commands + view models), call-time-only imports used to dodge cycles (use clear layers).
Run the prototype (node prototype/server.cjs or the GitHub Pages build) side by side with your build to compare feel: speed, pacing, how a week plays out.
Use the prototype's headless tools and autopilot as a baseline: e.g. how many survivors and how much food after 7 or 30 days on a seed; your sim should land in the same range for the slice systems.
Port slice-sized first: the prototype has 410 sim modules and ~208k lines grown over many features (malls, zoos, stadiums). The slice needs perhaps 25 of its ideas; the rest are later cards.
Respect the ADRs: AI groups follow the same rules as the player (0001) and base building decisions (0002) are already made; design commands and systems so AI can use them from the start.
